stem: After an uncomplicated diagnostic lumbar puncture, a client asks whether remaining flat for several hours is necessary solely to prevent a post-dural-puncture headache. Which response is most accurate?

options.A: Yes. Routine bed rest is recommended after lumbar puncture because it reduces the incidence of post-dural-puncture headache.
options.B: Yes. Because lying flat can relieve headache symptoms, routine bed rest should also be used to prevent the headache from developing.
options.C: Yes. Early mobilization should be avoided because bed rest has a proven prophylactic benefit over mobilization after lumbar puncture.
options.D: No. Routine bed rest is not recommended as prophylaxis; lying flat may provide temporary symptom relief if post-dural-puncture headache later develops.

rationale: The 2024 multisociety evidence-based guideline on post-dural-puncture headache states that routine bed rest is not recommended as prophylaxis against PDPH. It also notes that lying supine may provide temporary symptom relief when PDPH is already present, but this does not establish prophylactic benefit. Therefore D is correct. A and C incorrectly claim a preventive benefit from routine bed rest, and B incorrectly equates temporary symptom relief with prevention.
educational_objective: Distinguish prophylaxis from symptom relief after lumbar puncture: routine bed rest is not recommended solely to prevent post-dural-puncture headache.
source_organization: Multisociety International Working Group; published in Regional Anesthesia & Pain Medicine
source_document_title: Evidence-based clinical practice guidelines on postdural puncture headache: a consensus report from a multisociety international working group
source_version_date: Final journal version 2024; current guideline as accessed 2026-08-16
source_locator: Prophylactic measures > Bed rest: Recommendation — bed rest is not routinely recommended as prophylaxis against PDPH (Grade D, Moderate Level of Certainty). Conservative measures > Bed rest: temporary symptomatic relief may occur, but routine bed rest is not supported for treatment.
source_claim_supported: Routine bed rest should not be recommended solely to prevent PDPH after dural puncture; supine rest may transiently relieve symptoms once PDPH occurs but does not establish preventive benefit.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Reduction of Risk Potential, page 13: reducing complications related to treatments/procedures; evaluate client responses to procedures and treatments; use precautions to prevent complications associated with a procedure or diagnosis; educate client about treatments and procedures.
blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — prevention of complications after diagnostic procedure

source_original.stem: After an uncomplicated diagnostic lumbar puncture, a client asks whether remaining flat for several hours is necessary solely to prevent a post-dural-puncture headache. Which response is most accurate?

options.A: Remain flat for several hours after the procedure because prolonged bed rest has been shown to prevent post-dural-puncture headache after lumbar puncture.
options.B: Drink extra fluids specifically to prevent headache because aggressive hydration has been shown to stop cerebrospinal-fluid leakage after lumbar puncture.
options.C: Avoid upright activity until the next day because sitting or walking after lumbar puncture is known to increase persistent cerebrospinal-fluid leakage.
options.D: Prolonged bed rest is not shown to prevent post-puncture headache; follow postprocedure instructions and mobilize as clinically appropriate when allowed.

source_original.rationale: Current evidence does not support routine prolonged bed rest after lumbar puncture solely to prevent post-dural-puncture headache; Cochrane found that bed rest does not prevent the headache and may increase it, and extra fluids have not shown preventive benefit. Option D is correct. Option A incorrectly claims prolonged flat positioning is preventive. Option B overstates hydration as a preventive intervention. Option C incorrectly treats upright activity as a proven cause of persistent CSF leakage. Specific postprocedure instructions should still be followed for other clinical reasons.
source_original.source_detail: Cochrane Review CD009199 — Body position and intake of fluids for preventing headache after a lumbar puncture: routine bed rest after lumbar puncture does not prevent post-dural-puncture headache and may increase its occurrence; extra fluid intake has not shown preventive benefit. Routine prolonged flat positioning solely for prevention is not supported. Cochrane systematic review published 2016-03-07 remains the active evidence review at the cited source; currentness and absence of a superseding Cochrane conclusion rechecked 2026-08-15. Blueprint corrected to Reduction of Risk Potential because the item tests prevention of a complication after a diagnostic procedure, explicitly represented in the 2026 NCSBN test plan. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Physiological Integrity — Reduction of Risk Potential: diagnostic probability tools, laboratory/tumor-marker interpretation, ECG/lab monitoring and potential complications. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

correction_summary: Retained the stem, construct and key D but replaced the outdated 2016 Cochrane primary citation in the final payload with the newer 2024 multisociety evidence-based guideline. Rewrote distractors to remove unsupported CSF-leak mechanisms, unverified timing and aggressive-hydration claims; each distractor now directly tests the prevention-versus-symptom-relief distinction.

audit_findings.currentness: Newer guideline identified and used instead of relying on the 2016 Cochrane review; rechecked 2026-08-16
audit_findings.exact_locator: Guideline prophylactic measures > Bed rest recommendation; conservative measures > Bed rest
audit_findings.claim_audit: The correct answer and rationale state only the directly supported distinction: no routine prophylactic bed rest; supine position may temporarily relieve established PDPH symptoms.

distractor_audit.A: Falsely states routine bed rest reduces PDPH incidence.
distractor_audit.B: Incorrectly converts symptomatic relief into prophylactic efficacy.
distractor_audit.C: Falsely states bed rest has proven prophylactic benefit over mobilization.
distractor_audit.D: Matches the guideline recommendation and symptom-relief distinction.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only D is consistent with both the prophylaxis recommendation and the symptomatic-use evidence.
audit_findings.cueing: All options directly address bed rest after lumbar puncture; no option depends on an invented time threshold or mechanism.
audit_findings.blueprint: Reduction of Risk Potential — preventing complications related to a diagnostic procedure.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Re-audited currentness, recommendation wording, stem scope, each distractor, rationale, objective, blueprint and second-answer risk from zero; D remained uniquely best.
